title: ACCA SBR - Strategic Business Reporting
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ACCA SBR syllabus study guide. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: A newly appointed financial controller is instructed by the chief executive to record a material sale in the current year even though the customer order will not be fulfilled until the following year. Which fundamental principle of the ACCA Code of Ethics and Conduct is most directly threatened by this instruction?
options: Integrity
Confidentiality
Professional competence and due care
Objectivity
items.explanation: Integrity requires a member to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships, and deliberately recording a sale that has not occurred misstates the financial statements. Confidentiality concerns the use of information, professional competence concerns skill and diligence, and objectivity concerns bias rather than deliberate dishonesty.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: A reporting accountant holds a significant personal shareholding in the company that employs her, and the shares form the largest part of her personal wealth. Which threat to compliance with the fundamental principles does this create?
options: A familiarity threat
A self-interest threat
An intimidation threat
An advocacy threat
items.explanation: A self-interest threat arises when a financial or other interest in an outcome improperly influences judgement, which is the risk when the accountant's own wealth depends on reported results. Familiarity concerns closeness, advocacy concerns promoting a position, and intimidation concerns pressure exerted by others.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: Under the sustainability disclosure standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board, which body is responsible for issuing IFRS S1 and IFRS S2?
options: The IFRS Interpretations Committee
The Financial Accounting Standards Board
The International Sustainability Standards Board
The International Accounting Standards Board
items.explanation: IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 are issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board, which sits alongside the International Accounting Standards Board under the IFRS Foundation. The IASB issues IFRS Accounting Standards, the Interpretations Committee interprets them, and the FASB is the United States standard setter.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: Which statement best describes the objective of IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information?
options: To replace the financial statements with a single climate metric
To prescribe the exact numerical emission targets an entity must achieve
To require narrative reporting only, without any connection to financial performance
To require disclosure of sustainability-related risks and opportunities that is useful to primary users in making decisions about providing resources to the entity
items.explanation: IFRS S1 requires an entity to disclose material information about its sustainability-related risks and opportunities that is useful to primary users of general purpose financial reporting when assessing future cash flows and resource allocation. It does not replace the financial statements, set targets for the entity, or stand apart from financial performance.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: A professional accountant is served with a court order requiring the production of documents containing a client's confidential information. Which statement about the accountant's duty of confidentiality is correct?
options: Disclosure is permitted because the accountant has a professional duty to comply with the law
Disclosure is never permitted once confidentiality attaches to the information
The accountant must refuse until the client gives written consent
The accountant must disclose the information to the press to protect the public interest
items.explanation: The duty of confidentiality may be set aside where disclosure is required by law, for example under a court order, or where there is a professional right or duty to disclose. It is not absolute, and refusing a lawful order or disclosing to the press without authority is not justified.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: Which fundamental principle of the ACCA Code of Ethics and Conduct requires a member to maintain professional knowledge and skill at the level needed to ensure that a client or employer receives competent professional service?
options: Objectivity
Professional competence and due care
Integrity
Confidentiality
items.explanation: Professional competence and due care requires a member to attain and maintain professional knowledge and skill and to act diligently in accordance with applicable standards. Integrity concerns honesty, confidentiality concerns information, and objectivity concerns freedom from bias and conflicts of interest.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: A member in business is asked by the chief financial officer to leave out a material environmental provision so that the year-end profit figure meets an analyst forecast. What is the most appropriate course of action for the member?
options: Comply with the instruction because the chief financial officer is senior
Resign immediately without taking any other step
Decline to make the change and escalate the matter through the entity governance channels
Record the omission because profit is only a management estimate
items.explanation: The member should not be associated with misleading information, so the appropriate response is to decline and escalate the matter through the governance structure while documenting the concern. Complying breaches integrity, treating profit as a mere estimate misrepresents the provision, and resigning without escalation forgoes the chance to resolve the matter.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles
items.stem: Which reporting framework explains how an organisation creates value over time through the six capitals and is overseen within the IFRS Foundation?
options: IFRS S1
The GRI Sustainability Reporting Standards
The SASB Standards
The International Integrated Reporting Framework
items.explanation: The International Integrated Reporting Framework describes how an organisation uses and affects the six capitals to create value over the short, medium and long term. IFRS S1 and the SASB Standards address sustainability-related financial disclosures, and the GRI Standards focus on impact reporting.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Fundamental Ethical and Professional Principles

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: According to the IASB Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting, what is the objective of general purpose financial reporting?
options: To provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors in making decisions relating to providing resources to the entity
To report the entity taxable profit to the tax authorities
To enable management to control the day-to-day operations of the entity
To guarantee that the entity will remain a going concern for at least twelve months
items.explanation: The Conceptual Framework states that the objective of general purpose financial reporting is to provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors in making decisions relating to providing resources to the entity. Tax reporting, management control and any guarantee of survival are not that objective.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: Which pair of qualitative characteristics are described in the IASB Conceptual Framework as the fundamental characteristics that make financial information useful?
options: Prudence and neutrality
Relevance and faithful representation
Comparability and timeliness
Verifiability and understandability
items.explanation: The Conceptual Framework identifies relevance and faithful representation as the two fundamental qualitative characteristics. Comparability, timeliness, verifiability and understandability are enhancing characteristics, while prudence and neutrality are components of faithful representation.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: An entity sells a machine for 100,000 and, under the same contract, provides one year of maintenance that has a stand-alone selling price of 5,000. Control of the machine transfers at the start of the contract. Applying IFRS 15, how much revenue should be recognised when the machine is delivered?
items.explanation: IFRS 15 requires the transaction price of 100,000 to be allocated to each distinct performance obligation in proportion to its stand-alone selling price. The machine is worth 100,000 of the 105,000 total, so 95,000 is recognised at delivery and the remaining 5,000 is recognised as maintenance is provided.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: An entity enters a five-year lease with annual payments of 10,000 payable in arrears and an incremental borrowing rate of 5 percent. Which amount is closest to the initial lease liability recognised under IFRS 16?
items.explanation: IFRS 16 measures the lease liability at the present value of the lease payments, so 10,000 multiplied by the five-year annuity factor of 4.3295 equals about 43,295. Simply adding the payments gives 50,000, which ignores discounting.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: Which leases may a lessee elect, under IFRS 16, to account for as an expense on a straight-line basis rather than recognising a right-of-use asset and a lease liability?
options: Short-term leases of twelve months or less with no purchase option, and leases of low-value assets
All leases of property regardless of length
Leases of any asset where payments are made in arrears
Only leases that contain a bargain purchase option
items.explanation: IFRS 16 permits a lessee to apply the recognition exemptions to short-term leases, being twelve months or less without a purchase option, and to leases of low-value assets. The exemption is not available for all property leases, is unrelated to the timing of payments, and does not apply to leases with a purchase option.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: A debt instrument is held within a business model whose objective is to collect contractual cash flows, and those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest. Under IFRS 9, at which amount is the instrument measured?
options: The lower of cost and net realisable value
Amortised cost
Fair value through other comprehensive income
Fair value through profit or loss
items.explanation: IFRS 9 measures a financial asset at amortised cost only when it is held within a business model whose objective is to hold assets to collect contractual cash flows and the contractual terms give rise to cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest. The other measurement categories apply to different business models, and lower of cost and net realisable value is an inventory rule.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: At the reporting date a trade receivable is not credit-impaired but its credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition. Under IFRS 9, how should the loss allowance be measured?
options: At the full carrying amount of the receivable
At zero until the receivable is actually impaired
At an amount equal to lifetime expected credit losses
At an amount equal to twelve-month expected credit losses
items.explanation: IFRS 9 requires the loss allowance to equal twelve-month expected credit losses for assets whose credit risk has not increased significantly, but lifetime expected credit losses once credit risk has increased significantly. The full carrying amount and a nil allowance are not permitted measures under the expected credit loss model.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: Under IFRS 17 Insurance Contracts, which component represents the unearned profit that the entity recognises as it provides insurance coverage?
options: The risk adjustment for non-financial risk
The fulfilment cash flows
The insurance revenue
The contractual service margin
items.explanation: The contractual service margin is the unearned profit of a group of insurance contracts that is recognised in profit or loss as the entity provides coverage. The risk adjustment compensates for uncertainty, fulfilment cash flows combine the present value of estimates and the risk adjustment, and insurance revenue is the amount recognised, not the unearned profit itself.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: An entity faces a legal claim relating to a past event and its lawyers advise that an outflow of 100,000 is probable and can be measured reliably. Under IAS 37, how should the entity account for the claim?
options: Recognise a provision of 100,000 and disclose the contingency
Recognise a contingent liability only, with no entry in the financial statements
Recognise a provision of 60,000 reflecting the probability of loss
Ignore the claim because it has not yet been settled
items.explanation: IAS 37 requires a provision to be recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow of resources is probable, and the amount can be estimated reliably. A contingent liability is only disclosed when the outflow is not probable, and provisions are not scaled down by the probability of loss.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: Under IAS 38 Intangible Assets, which expenditure may be capitalised as an internally generated intangible asset?
options: Training costs for staff who will operate a new process
Development costs that meet all of the recognition criteria, including technical feasibility and the intention to complete
All research costs incurred before a project is approved
Advertising and promotion costs for a new brand
items.explanation: IAS 38 requires research costs to be expensed and permits development costs to be capitalised only when the entity can demonstrate technical feasibility, the intention and ability to complete, probable future economic benefits and reliable measurement. Advertising, promotion and training costs are always expensed.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: At the reporting date the carrying amount of an item of plant is 100,000 and its tax base is 70,000, and the tax rate is 25 percent. Which amount is the deferred tax liability?
items.explanation: A taxable temporary difference of 100,000 minus 70,000, which is 30,000, multiplied by the 25 percent tax rate gives a deferred tax liability of 7,500. The figure 30,000 is the temporary difference before tax, while 25,000 and 17,500 apply the rate to the wrong base.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: The Financial Reporting Framework
items.stem: Under the IASB Conceptual Framework, which statement about the going concern assumption is correct?
options: The going concern assumption guarantees that an entity will trade profitably
The going concern assumption replaces the need for faithful representation
The going concern assumption applies only to entities with no borrowings
Financial statements are normally prepared on a going concern basis unless management either intends to liquidate the entity or has no realistic alternative but to do so
items.explanation: The Conceptual Framework states that financial statements are normally prepared on the going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so. It does not guarantee profits, does not replace any qualitative characteristic, and is not limited to entities without debt.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - The Financial Reporting Framework

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: Under IFRS 10 Consolidated Financial Statements, an investor controls an investee when it has which combination of elements?
options: Power over the investee, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use its power to affect those returns
Ownership of more than fifty percent of the voting shares alone
The right to receive dividends and a seat on the board
A contractual right to manage the investee's day-to-day operations only
items.explanation: IFRS 10 defines control as power over the investee combined with exposure or rights to variable returns and the ability to use that power to affect the amount of those returns. Majority voting rights are only one way to obtain power, and neither dividend rights nor day-to-day management alone establishes control.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: Entity A holds 45 percent of the voting shares of Entity B but has a contractual right to appoint four of the five directors of B, who direct the relevant activities. How should A account for its interest in B?
options: Account for B as a joint operation because the directors are appointed by contract
Consolidate B as a subsidiary because A has power over the relevant activities
Account for B as an associate using the equity method because A holds less than half
Measure B as a simple investment at fair value through profit or loss
items.explanation: IFRS 10 focuses on power rather than a shareholding threshold, so a contractual right to appoint the majority of the board that directs the relevant activities gives A control and requires consolidation. Holding less than half the shares does not by itself prevent control, so neither the equity method nor fair value applies.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: A parent acquires 80 percent of a subsidiary for 800,000 when the fair value of the subsidiary's identifiable net assets is 900,000. The non-controlling interest is measured at its proportionate share of net assets. What is the goodwill on acquisition?
items.explanation: Goodwill equals the consideration of 800,000 plus the non-controlling interest of 20 percent of 900,000, which is 180,000, less the 900,000 fair value of net assets, giving 80,000. Comparing the consideration only with the full net assets ignores the non-controlling interest and gives a misleading figure.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: A parent acquires 80 percent of a subsidiary for 800,000 when the fair value of identifiable net assets is 900,000 and the non-controlling interest is measured at its fair value of 220,000. What is the goodwill on acquisition?
items.explanation: When the non-controlling interest is measured at fair value, goodwill equals consideration of 800,000 plus non-controlling interest of 220,000 less net assets of 900,000, which is 120,000. The higher figure compared with the proportionate method represents the goodwill attributed to the non-controlling interest.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: Contingent consideration payable by an acquirer in a business combination is classified as a financial liability. How is it accounted for in subsequent periods under IFRS 3?
options: It is remeasured to fair value at each reporting date with changes recognised in profit or loss
It is held at the original amount until the contingency is resolved
It is remeasured through other comprehensive income
It is written off immediately against retained earnings
items.explanation: IFRS 3 requires contingent consideration classified as a liability to be remeasured to fair value at each reporting date, with changes generally recognised in profit or loss. It is not fixed at the original amount, not routed through other comprehensive income, and not written off against retained earnings.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: An acquirer incurs fees for legal advice and due diligence work in connection with a business combination. Under IFRS 3, how are these acquisition-related costs treated?
options: They are recognised directly in other comprehensive income
They are expensed in the period in which they are incurred
They are capitalised as part of goodwill
They are added to the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired
items.explanation: IFRS 3 requires acquisition-related costs, such as due diligence and legal fees, to be expensed as incurred rather than included in the cost of the combination. Capitalising them in goodwill or net assets, or reporting them in other comprehensive income, is not permitted.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: In a consolidated statement of financial position prepared under IFRS 10, how is the non-controlling interest presented?
options: As a deduction from goodwill on acquisition
As a long-term investment in the assets section
Within equity, separately from the equity attributable to the owners of the parent
As a liability because it represents an outside claim
items.explanation: IFRS 10 requires the non-controlling interest to be presented within equity but separately from the equity of the owners of the parent. It is not a liability, is not netted against goodwill, and is not an asset.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: An investor holds 30 percent of the ordinary shares of another entity and exercises significant influence over its operating and financial policies. Under IAS 28, how should the investor account for this investment?
options: At fair value through profit or loss in all cases
By full consolidation of the investee line by line
At the lower of cost and market value
Using the equity method, initially at cost and then adjusted for the investor's share of profit or loss
items.explanation: IAS 28 requires an investment in an associate, over which the investor has significant influence, to be accounted for using the equity method, initially at cost and adjusted for the share of the associate's results and other changes. Full consolidation applies only to subsidiaries, and the other measurement bases are not used.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: An investor acquires 30 percent of an associate for 300,000. During the year the associate reports profit of 100,000 and pays dividends of 20,000. What is the carrying amount of the investment under the equity method?
items.explanation: Under the equity method the investment starts at cost of 300,000, increases by 30 percent of the 100,000 profit, which is 30,000, and decreases by 30 percent of the 20,000 dividend, which is 6,000, giving 324,000. Adding the whole profit or ignoring the dividend gives the wrong carrying amount.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: An investor's share of an associate's losses has reduced the carrying amount of the investment to nil and the investor has no legal or constructive obligation to fund further losses. How should the investor account for additional losses under IAS 28?
options: Continue reducing the investment into a negative carrying amount
Recognise no further losses and disclose the unrecognised share
Recognise the losses as a liability regardless of any obligation
Recognise the losses against retained earnings as an adjustment
items.explanation: Under the equity method the investor discontinues recognising its share of further losses once the carrying amount of the investment is reduced to nil, unless the investor has incurred a legal or constructive obligation. The unrecognised share of losses is disclosed, and no negative carrying amount is created.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: During consolidation, a parent has sold inventory to its subsidiary at a profit and some of that inventory remains unsold at the reporting date. How is the unrealised profit treated in the consolidated financial statements?
options: It is deferred and recognised only when the subsidiary itself sells the inventory
It is left in consolidated profit because the transaction was at arm's length
It is eliminated against inventory and the related profit, with any non-controlling interest share adjusted when the sale was upstream
It is recognised immediately as a consolidated gain
items.explanation: Intra-group profits are recognised only when the goods are sold to parties outside the group, so the unrealised profit is eliminated from inventory and the related profit. For an upstream sale, meaning subsidiary to parent, the elimination is shared with the non-controlling interest.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: A parent sells inventory to its subsidiary for 100,000 that had cost the parent 80,000. At the reporting date half of the inventory is still held by the subsidiary. Ignoring tax, what is the unrealised profit to be eliminated on consolidation?
options: Nil
items.explanation: The profit on the intra-group sale is 20,000 and only half of the inventory remains in the group, so the unrealised profit to be eliminated is 10,000. Eliminating the full 20,000 would be wrong because half has been sold outside the group, and nil ignores the adjustment entirely.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: When a parent loses control of a subsidiary, how is the gain or loss on disposal measured under IFRS 10?
options: As the difference between the proceeds plus the fair value of any retained interest and the carrying amount of the net assets and recognised non-controlling interest, with related amounts recycled from other comprehensive income
As the difference between the proceeds and the original cost of the investment only
As the difference between the proceeds and the parent's share of share capital
Only through other comprehensive income with no amount recognised in profit or loss
items.explanation: On loss of control IFRS 10 requires the gain or loss to be measured using the proceeds plus the fair value of any retained interest, less the carrying amount of the net assets and non-controlling interest, with amounts previously recognised in other comprehensive income recycled. The recognition is in profit or loss, not solely in equity.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: A parent disposes of its entire 100 percent holding in a subsidiary for 500,000. At the disposal date the net assets of the subsidiary are 400,000 and goodwill of 30,000 had been recognised on acquisition. What is the gain or loss on disposal?
options: Loss of 30,000
Gain of 70,000
Gain of 100,000
Gain of 30,000
items.explanation: The gain on disposal is the proceeds of 500,000 less the carrying amount of the net assets of 400,000 and the goodwill of 30,000, giving 70,000. Comparing the proceeds only with the net assets gives 100,000 and ignores the goodwill written off with the subsidiary.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: An entity increases its holding in another company from 20 percent, previously an associate, to 60 percent, giving it control. How is the previously held 20 percent interest treated on the business combination?
options: It is derecognised against retained earnings with no gain or loss
It is combined with goodwill and amortised over ten years
It is remeasured to fair value at the acquisition date with any gain or loss recognised in profit or loss
It is carried forward at its original equity-method carrying amount
items.explanation: IFRS 3 treats a step acquisition as the acquirer obtaining control, so the previously held interest is remeasured to fair value at the acquisition date and the resulting gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss. The old carrying amount is not simply carried forward, and identifiable gains are not deferred.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: Under IAS 21 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates, how is an entity's functional currency determined?
options: It must always be the currency of the country in which the entity is incorporated
It is the currency chosen freely by management for presentation purposes
It is the currency in which the majority of the shareholders are based
It is the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates
items.explanation: IAS 21 defines the functional currency as the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates, which is normally the currency that mainly influences sales prices and costs. It is not automatically the incorporation currency or a free management choice, and shareholder location is not the determinant.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: When translating the financial statements of a foreign operation into a different presentation currency under IAS 21, at which rate are assets and liabilities translated?
options: At the closing rate at the reporting date
At the historical rate for the transaction date of each item
At the average rate for the period
At the rate at the date the foreign operation was acquired
items.explanation: IAS 21 requires assets and liabilities to be translated at the closing rate at the reporting date, while income and expenses are translated at the rates at the dates of the transactions, often approximated by the average rate. Exchange differences are recognised in other comprehensive income.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups
items.stem: An entity whose functional currency is the pound holds a receivable of USD 100,000 when the exchange rate is one pound to 1.20 dollars. At the reporting date the rate is one pound to 1.25 dollars. Which exchange difference arises?
options: No exchange difference because the receivable is not yet settled
An exchange loss of approximately 3,333 pounds
An exchange gain of approximately 3,333 pounds
An exchange gain of approximately 4,167 pounds
items.explanation: The receivable was recorded at 100,000 divided by 1.20, which is 83,333 pounds, and is restated at 100,000 divided by 1.25, which is 80,000 pounds. The pound value falls by about 3,333 pounds, which is a loss because a foreign-currency asset weakened in pound terms as the pound strengthened.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Reporting the Financial Performance of Groups

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: A company reports profit before interest and tax of 500,000 and capital employed of 2,500,000. What is the return on capital employed?
options: 25 percent
10 percent
20 percent
5 percent
items.explanation: Return on capital employed is profit before interest and tax divided by capital employed, so 500,000 divided by 2,500,000 equals 20 percent. The other figures result from inverting the ratio or comparing the profit with a different base.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: A company has debt of 400,000 and equity of 600,000. On a debt-to-equity basis, what is the gearing ratio?
options: 40.0 percent
150.0 percent
60.0 percent
66.7 percent
items.explanation: Gearing on a debt-to-equity basis is debt divided by equity, so 400,000 divided by 600,000 equals 66.7 percent. Dividing debt by total capital gives 40.0 percent, which is a different definition of gearing.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: A company reports earnings before interest and tax of 600,000 and interest expense of 150,000. What is the interest cover?
options: 4.0 times
0.25 times
4.5 times
3.0 times
items.explanation: Interest cover is earnings before interest and tax divided by interest expense, so 600,000 divided by 150,000 equals 4.0 times. The value 0.25 times is the reciprocal and would indicate that interest exceeds earnings, which is the wrong way round.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: A company has a net profit margin of 8 percent, an asset turnover of 1.5 times and an equity multiplier of 2.0. Using the DuPont decomposition, what is the return on equity?
options: 9.5 percent
24 percent
12 percent
16 percent
items.explanation: The three-part DuPont identity multiplies net profit margin, asset turnover and the equity multiplier, so 8 percent times 1.5 times 2.0 equals 24 percent. Omitting or mis-multiplying one factor produces the lower distractors.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: A company reports higher revenue and profit than the prior year, but operating cash flow has fallen sharply and days sales outstanding has increased. Which conclusion is most consistent with these trends?
options: The increase in profit is fully supported by cash generation
The fall in operating cash flow is caused by higher depreciation
The quality of earnings has deteriorated because profits are not being converted into cash
The company has become more efficient at collecting cash from customers
items.explanation: Rising profit alongside falling operating cash flow and longer collection periods suggests that sales are being recognised without corresponding cash collection, which weakens the quality of earnings. It is inconsistent with improved collection, with full cash support for profit, and with higher depreciation, which would be added back to operating cash flow.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: Under IFRS 8 Operating Segments, how are reportable operating segments identified?
options: On the basis of the separate legal entities within the group
On the basis of the geographical regions chosen by the auditors
On the basis of the industry classification of each customer
On the basis of the internal reports regularly reviewed by the entity chief operating decision maker to allocate resources and assess performance
items.explanation: IFRS 8 uses a management approach, so operating segments are based on the internal reports reviewed by the chief operating decision maker. Legal structure, auditor-chosen regions and customer industry classifications are not the basis for identifying segments.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: An entity's financial statements are prepared on a going concern basis but there are material uncertainties that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue. What does IAS 1 require?
options: Disclose the material uncertainties so that users can understand the judgement
Change the basis of preparation to a break-up basis automatically
Remove the going concern assumption without any disclosure
Make no disclosure because the going concern basis has been retained
items.explanation: IAS 1 requires an entity to disclose material uncertainties related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern. The going concern basis is retained, and a break-up basis applies only when liquidation is intended or unavoidable.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: After the reporting date but before the financial statements are authorised for issue, a court judgment confirms the amount of an obligation that existed at the reporting date. Under IAS 10, how is this event classified?
options: As a prior period error to be corrected retrospectively
As an adjusting event that requires the financial statements to be adjusted
As a non-adjusting event that requires only disclosure
As an event that has no effect on the financial statements
items.explanation: IAS 10 treats an event after the reporting date that provides evidence of conditions existing at that date as an adjusting event, so the recognised amount is updated. A non-adjusting event reflects conditions arising after the reporting date, and a court outcome confirming an existing obligation is not a prior period error.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: A factory is destroyed by a fire after the reporting date but before the financial statements are authorised for issue. Under IAS 10, how should this event be treated?
options: As an adjusting event recognised through opening retained earnings
As a change in accounting policy applied retrospectively
As a non-adjusting event, with disclosure if it is material
As an adjusting event that restates the carrying amount of the factory
items.explanation: The fire indicates a condition that arose after the reporting date, so IAS 10 classifies it as a non-adjusting event, with disclosure required when it is material. It does not restate the asset, is not processed through opening retained earnings, and is not a change in accounting policy.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements introduces a required structure for the statement of profit or loss. Which categories of income and expenses does it require an entity to present?
options: Only operating and non-operating categories
Current and non-current categories only
Revenue and capital categories only
Operating, investing and financing categories, plus income taxes and discontinued operations
items.explanation: IFRS 18 requires income and expenses to be classified into operating, investing and financing categories, with income taxes and discontinued operations presented separately. The older flexible presentation of only operating and non-operating items is replaced, and current and non-current categories are a balance sheet classification.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: IFRS 18 introduces requirements for management-defined performance measures. Which measure qualifies as a management-defined performance measure?
options: A subtotal of income and expenses used in public communications outside the financial statements that is not required or defined by IFRS Accounting Standards
Any subtotal that IFRS Accounting Standards require to be presented
The gross profit subtotal required by the standard
Any ratio disclosed in the notes to the financial statements
items.explanation: IFRS 18 defines a management-defined performance measure as a subtotal of income and expenses that management uses in public communications outside the financial statements but that is not specified or required by IFRS Accounting Standards. Subtotals required by the standards and ordinary ratios are not management-defined measures.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information

items.domain: Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
items.stem: Recent amendments to IAS 7 and IFRS 7 require disclosure about supplier finance arrangements. What is the primary objective of these disclosure requirements?
options: To require the arrangements to be measured at fair value through profit or loss
To disclose the terms and carrying amounts of the arrangements and their effects on the entity cash flows and exposure to liquidity risk
To require the arrangements to be recognised as borrowings in all cases
To prohibit the use of supplier finance arrangements
items.explanation: The amendments require qualitative and quantitative disclosure of supplier finance arrangements, including their terms, the carrying amounts involved and their cash-flow and liquidity-risk effects, so that users can assess the impact. They do not reclassify all arrangements as borrowings, prohibit them, or impose fair value measurement.
items.reference: ACCA SBR Syllabus Study Guide - Interpretation and Disclosure of Financial Information
